extracted.intended_audience: students, poets, and literary critics studying poetic craft (epic and tragic poetry) and Aristotle's Poetics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating epic (epopœia) and tragic poetry according to Aristotelian principles: selection of subject, structure (parts), appropriate verse, treatment of marvel/absurdity, length/unity, and diction. Useful for poets deciding form and critics assessing works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity / single action for tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither Homer's Iliad nor Odyssey can furnish but one Subject for Tragedy, or two at most.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose one simple action (or at most two) as the subject of a tragedy; if drawing from larger epics shorten the time and focus to isolate a single action (e.g., the quarrel between Achilles and Agamemnon or the return/absence episodes in the Odyssey).

rubrics_metrics.name: Epopeia shares the same parts as tragedy (except music/decoration)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Epopeia has also the same Parts as Tragedy (Fable, Diction, Manners, Sentiments, Remembrances, Peripeties, and Passions) except Music and the Decoration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or evaluating an epic, check for these structural components; musical elements and stage decoration are irrelevant to epic as it imitates by recitation rather than theatrical performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of epic (simple/complex; moral/pathetic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Epopœia must be Simple or Implex (complex); Moral or Pathetick — it must have one of these four conditions since imitation of an action requires one of these characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the epic's action will be primarily simple (single plotline) or complex (with peripeties/remembrances), and whether its dominant tone will be moral (didactic/virtue-model) or pathetic (focused on suffering/death). Use this classification to shape plot and tone (e.g., Iliad = simple & pathetic; Odyssey = complex & moral).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentiments must match diction
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sentiments ought to be as fine as the Diction: Homer excelled in mixing both with prudence and judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft sentiments (ideas, moral/philosophical content) to be as polished and appropriate as the diction; strong sentiment with weak diction (or vice versa) diminishes poetic quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length / unity of view (beginning and end under one view)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is sufficient if we can have the beginning and end under one View. The Recitation of an Epic Poem should take up no more time than the Representation of the different sorts of Tragedy which are acted in one Day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit the poem's scope so readers/listeners can retain the idea of beginning-to-end in one view (traditionally a single day's recitation). Shorten plans compared to sprawling ancient cycles; if the beginning is forgotten before the end, the poem is too long.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic may be longer than tragedy due to narration
rubrics_metrics.description: Epopœia has this Property, That it may be of a much larger extent than Tragedy: as narration can show several things done at the same time and in different places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use narration to expand scope (multiple simultaneous scenes, wide geography), but keep the central unity and avoid extraneous episodes that obscure the main action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate verse for epic: heroic/hexameter
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience shows that the Heroick (hexameter) is the only one that agrees with it: Heroick Verse is the most grave and pompous and admits strange words and metaphors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer hexameter (heroic verse) for long epic narrative to achieve gravitas and to allow elevated diction and metaphors. Avoid using verse types that produce movement/colloquial tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verse for action and motion: iambic and tetrameter
rubrics_metrics.description: The Iambick and Tetrameter Verses are proper to give Motion: the Tetrameter is good for Dancing, and the Iambick for Action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use iambic/tetrameter for dramatic/action-oriented pieces (tragedy, lyric motion); avoid them for epic narrative where majesty is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mix verse types in a long poem
rubrics_metrics.description: It would be more Ridiculous to mix them altogether, as Cheremon has done; therefore nobody has undertaken to make a long Poem in any other sort of Verse than the Hexameter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid mixing hexameter with iambic/tetrameter within the same long epic; such mixture undermines gravitas and can be jarring and ridiculous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marvelous and extravagance permitted (esp. in epic)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Marvellous ought to be in Tragedy, but much more in Epopœia, in which it goes even to the Extravagant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic may embrace marvelous or extravagant elements more freely than stage drama because narration can make the implausible agreeable; use marvel selectively to delight and astonish rather than to break the poem's internal plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer impossible but plausible-seeming incidents over incredible possibles
rubrics_metrics.description: The Poet ought rather to choose Impossibilities, provided they have a Resemblance to the Truth, than the Possible, which are Incredible with all their Possibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing events, prefer imaginatively 'impossible' incidents that feel believable within the poem's logic to technically possible events that strain credulity; plausibility of likeness to truth matters more than ontological possibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every incident ought to have its causes and reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: All the Incidents of a Poem ought to have their Causes and Reasons; and if that be impossible, then that which is unreasonable must be out of the Subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure plot events are motivated and connected by causal reasoning; if something cannot be causally justified within the subject, it should be excluded from the central action (example: avoid central unexplained ignorance like Oedipus's if it cannot be made plausible).

rubrics_metrics.name: Admit unavoidable absurdities if they make the rest more probable
rubrics_metrics.description: If some places which appear absurd cannot be avoided, they must be admitted, especially if they contribute to render the rest more probable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow limited absurd or implausible elements when necessary to achieve greater overall plausibility or dramatic effect, but minimize and conceal them within admirable or distracting material (Homer's technique).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hide defects under admirable ornamentation (Homer's method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Homer has hid his Abſurdities under an Infinity of admirable things, with which he has sprinkled all that part of his Poem, and which are as so many Charms to hinder our perceiving that defect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rich, admirable detail and ornamentation to divert attention from minor improbabilities; strong descriptive/dictional brilliance can mask structural weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve ornaments of diction for weak parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Thus ought we to reserve all the Ornaments of the Diction for these weak parts: Those that have either good Sentiments, or Manners, have no occasion for them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid over-embellishing parts that are already strong in sentiment or characterization; reserve heightened diction and rhetorical ornamentation to shore up weaker passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid resemblance among episodes within a work
rubrics_metrics.description: Narration allows many Episodes, but if a piece has many Episodes they must not resemble each other; resemblance of Episodes is a usual cause of ill success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design varied episodes in epic so they do not repeat structure or effect; repetitive episodes reduce interest and cause audience fatigue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify Iliad vs Odyssey by essential characters (simplicity/pathetic vs complexity/moral)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Iliad is Simple and Pathetick; the Odyssey Implex and Moral: simplicity and pathos characterize the Iliad from start to finish, while the Odyssey is complex with peripeties/remembrances and moral instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When modeling or critiquing, recognize which qualities should dominate: a pathos-driven, single-action epic (Iliad model) versus a moral, episodic, multi-incident epic (Odyssey model).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet should minimize authorial intrusion; show characters with manners
rubrics_metrics.description: The Poet ought to say little himself, for in that he is not an Imitator. Homer says little himself but introduces presently some of his Persons... for every thing in his Poem has Manners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor showing over telling: let characters' behavior ('manners') convey moral and narrative content rather than explanatory authorial commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match verse choice to rhetorical needs: hexameter admits elevated diction and strange metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: Heroick Verse is the most Grave and Pompous, so it has a particular way of admitting strange Words and Metaphors, and that Imitation which consists in Narration uses them much more than all the others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hexameter (or analogous elevated meters) when you intend to deploy grand metaphors, unusual diction, and pompous tone; expect greater tolerance for lexical strangeness in such verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize that meanest parts require ornaments
rubrics_metrics.description: The meanest Parts require all the Ornaments of Diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply rhetorial/dictional ornamentation particularly to less inherently interesting parts of the poem to elevate them and maintain overall quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action duration depends on degree of violence
rubrics_metrics.description: If an Action is Violent and full of Passion, it has less duration; for that which is violent cannot endure long.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When mapping the poem's temporal scope, compress violent, passion-driven actions into shorter narrative durations; gentler actions may legitimately span longer durations (use this to plan pacing—e.g., Iliad concentrates days, Odyssey spans years).

rubrics_metrics.name: Narration permits showing several things at once (use to increase scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Narration gives the Poet an opportunity to represent several things which are done at the same time, and in different Places, and which being proper to the Subject, give this Poem such an Extent that the other (tragedy) cannot have.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit narration to portray simultaneous or spatially dispersed events that enhance the grandeur and variety of the epic, while keeping them thematically relevant to the subject.
